title: How Common Are Primes?
short: The prime number theorem: there are about x/ln x primes up to x. Primes thin out, and n! + 2, …, n! + n is a run of n − 1 composite numbers.
trouble: Students read x/ln x as the exact count. It is an estimate (78,498 primes are below one million; the estimate gives about 72,382), and its relative error shrinks as x grows.

blocks.html: There are infinitely many primes, but how many up to a given point? Write $\pi(x)$ for the number of primes $p \le x$ (this $\pi$ has nothing to do with $3.14159\dots$). So $\pi(10) = 4$ and $\pi(100) = 25$.

The prime number theorem (proved in 1896 by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin): $$\pi(x) \sim \frac{x}{\ln x}, \quad\text{meaning}\quad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\pi(x)}{x / \ln x} = 1.$$ Here $\ln$ is the natural logarithm. An equivalent way to say it: near a large number $x$, roughly one number in $\ln x$ is prime.

blocks.name: nt-sieve
blocks.cap: The exact count $\pi(x)$ (a staircase) and the estimate $x/\ln x$. The gap between them grows, but the ratio creeps toward 1.

blocks.html: Why a logarithm? Each extra digit makes primes a little rarer, by about the same amount. Among the 900 three-digit numbers there are $168 - 25 = 143$ primes, about 1 in 6.3, and $\ln 500 \approx 6.2$. Among the 900,000 six-digit numbers there are $78{,}498 - 9{,}592 = 68{,}906$ primes, about 1 in 13, and $\ln 550{,}000 \approx 13.2$. The density $1/\ln x$ captures this slow thinning. (The proof uses complex analysis and is far beyond this course.)

blocks.title: Using the estimate
blocks.q: Estimate $\pi(10^{6})$ with $x/\ln x$, and compare with the true value $78{,}498$.
steps: The estimate is about $6{,}100$ too low, roughly $8\%$ of the true count. At $10^{9}$ it is $5\%$ low.

blocks.title: Long gaps between primes
steps: The same trick with $n! + 2, \dots, n! + n$ gives $n - 1$ composites in a row, so gaps between primes can be as long as you like.

blocks.title: Why cryptographers care
blocks.q: About what fraction of 100-digit numbers are prime?
steps: Near $x = 10^{100}$, about one number in $\ln 10^{100} = 100 \ln 10 \approx 230$ is prime.
So a random 100-digit odd number is prime with probability about $2/230 = 1/115$: a computer finds one after about a hundred tries. RSA keys are made this way.

blocks.html: Treating $x/\ln x$ as the exact count. It is an estimate: $\pi(10^{6}) = 78{,}498$, while $10^{6}/\ln 10^{6} \approx 72{,}382$. The theorem promises only that the ratio tends to 1, so the relative error shrinks. The difference itself keeps growing.
$\pi(x) \sim x/\ln x$: the ratio tends to 1. Near $x$, about one number in $\ln x$ is prime; primes thin out, slowly.
